title: One, Two, Many
theme: Number prefixes uni-/mono-, bi-, tri- and multi-
objectives: I can explain what uni-, mono-, bi-, tri-, and multi- add to a word.
I can use a prefix and a base to work out the meaning of a new word.
I can tell when a number prefix helps and when a word has a meaning that goes beyond its parts.
I can write about agreements and decisions using words that count sides, voices, and parts.
rationale: Number prefixes appear in civics (unanimous, bilateral, bipartisan), literature (trilogy, monologue), economics (monopoly), and everyday description (monotonous, multifaceted). Each word here has a visible number part, so students can practice splitting a word, naming the count, and checking the result against the real meaning. The unit also teaches honesty about word parts: monopoly and trilogy carry meanings that the prefix alone does not give, and multitude is taught as a whole word. The words are grouped by what they count: sides and voices in agreements, one-of-a-kind voices and controls, and three or many.

words.def: Agreed on by everyone, with no one disagreeing.
words.ex: The vote to rename the library was unanimous; not one hand stayed down.
words.ex2: The jury's unanimous decision came after only an hour of discussion.
words.nonExample: A vote that passes 20 to 5 is not unanimous.

segs.m: full of; having the quality of

morph.note: The i of uni- is dropped before anim. Together the parts suggest 'of one mind'.

apps.academic: A unanimous vote means every voter chose the same option.
apps.spoken: It was unanimous: we're all going to the beach.
apps.writing: Use unanimous only when no one disagrees; use overwhelming when most do.

cloze.s: The class was ___ in choosing the red banner; all twenty-six students raised a hand.

cloze2.s: Not one person voted against the plan, so the result was ___.

misuse.s: The vote was unanimous, with half the members voting against it.
misuse.why: Unanimous means everyone agrees; half voting no is the opposite.

visual.alt: A ballot box next to a row of raised hands.

words.def: Done or decided by only one side, without the agreement of the others.
words.ex: The coach made a unilateral decision to cancel practice and never asked the team.
words.ex2: The neighboring country complained about the unilateral change to the border rules.
words.nonExample: A plan that every group discussed and signed is not unilateral.

apps.academic: A unilateral action is taken by one government or group without the others' consent.
apps.spoken: You can't make a unilateral decision about our group project.
apps.writing: Use unilateral to show that one side decided alone, and say who was left out.

cloze.s: Instead of asking the group, Dev made a ___ decision to move the meeting to Friday.

cloze2.s: The company's ___ change to the rules was announced after no customer had been asked.

misuse.s: Both countries talked it over for weeks and then signed a unilateral agreement together.
misuse.why: Unilateral means one side alone; an agreement both sides discuss and sign is not unilateral.

visual.alt: A raised finger above a rolled-up scroll.

words.frame: A unilateral decision is unfair when ___.

words.def: Involving two sides, groups, or countries.
words.ex: The two countries signed a bilateral agreement to share the water of a border river.
words.ex2: Bilateral talks between the schools produced a plan for a shared playing field.
words.nonExample: A treaty signed by twelve nations is not bilateral.

apps.academic: A bilateral trade agreement is made between exactly two countries.
apps.spoken: It's a bilateral deal, so both of us have to agree.
apps.writing: Use bilateral when exactly two parties are involved; use multilateral for more.

cloze.s: Because exactly two nations had to approve every term, the treaty was ___.

cloze2.s: The ___ talks between the two schools included three students from each side.

misuse.s: The bilateral treaty was a single agreement among twelve nations that all joined at once.
misuse.why: Bilateral involves two sides; twelve nations make a treaty with many sides.

visual.alt: A handshake in front of a globe.

words.frame: A bilateral agreement between ___ and ___ might cover ___.

words.def: Supported by or involving members of two major political parties.
words.ex: A bipartisan group of lawmakers, five from each party, wrote the new park law together.
words.ex2: The bill passed because it had bipartisan support, not just votes from one party.
words.nonExample: A bill backed by only one party is not bipartisan.

segs.m: a supporter of a party or cause

apps.academic: A bipartisan committee has members from both major parties so that more voters are represented.
apps.spoken: They worked out a bipartisan plan both sides could live with.
apps.writing: Use bipartisan for cooperation between two political parties, not for any two people.

cloze.s: Members from both major parties wrote the bill together, so it earned ___ support.

cloze2.s: Hoping for ___ cooperation, the governor invited leaders of both parties to write the plan together.

misuse.s: The bipartisan committee included only members of a single political party.
misuse.why: Bipartisan involves two parties; a committee from one party is not bipartisan.

visual.alt: A government building above a handshake.

words.frame: A bipartisan solution would need ___ from both parties.

src.note: Taught as the U.S. civics term for two major parties.

words.def: A set of three books, films, or plays that tell a connected story.
words.ex: Nia read the whole fantasy trilogy in one summer, finishing the third book on the last day of vacation.
words.ex2: The director filmed his space trilogy over nine years.
words.nonExample: A single short poem is not a trilogy.

segs.m: words or writing; a set of works

words.rel: a story told in three parts

apps.academic: In a trilogy, each book usually adds to one larger conflict.
apps.spoken: Have you read the whole trilogy or just the first book?
apps.writing: Use trilogy only for exactly three connected works.

cloze.s: The author finished the third and final book of her ___ and began a new series.

cloze2.s: Each film in the ___ ended with a clue that led straight into the next story.

misuse.s: A trilogy is a single short poem with four lines.
misuse.why: A trilogy is a set of three connected works, not one short poem.

visual.alt: Three books in a row, one red, one green, and one blue.

words.frame: A good trilogy I know is ___ because ___.

words.def: Complete control of a product or service by one company, with no competition.
words.ex: With the only bus line in town, the company held a monopoly on public transportation.
words.ex2: A monopoly can raise prices because customers have nowhere else to buy.
words.nonExample: Five bakeries competing on one street do not have a monopoly.

morph.note: Here poly comes from a Greek word meaning to sell. It is not the prefix poly- meaning many.

apps.academic: Governments sometimes break up a monopoly so that other companies can compete.
apps.spoken: That store has a monopoly on the only pizza in town.
apps.writing: Use monopoly for one seller controlling a market, not for any large company.

cloze.s: Because the water company was the only one allowed in town, it held a ___ and could set any price.

cloze2.s: The streaming company tried to build a ___ by buying every rival, leaving customers with no other choice.

misuse.s: Five bakeries competed fiercely on the same street, and each one held a monopoly.
misuse.why: A monopoly means one seller with no rivals; five competing bakeries are the opposite.

visual.alt: A tall office building with a padlock in front.

words.frame: A monopoly is a problem for customers because ___.

words.def: Boring because it stays the same, with no change or variety.
words.ex: The long, flat highway was monotonous, mile after mile of identical fields.
words.ex2: Her monotonous voice made even the most exciting story sound dull.
words.nonExample: A day full of new places and surprises is not monotonous.

segs.m: full of; having the quality of

morph.note: The final e of tone is dropped before -ous.

apps.academic: A monotonous speaker uses almost no change in pitch, so listeners lose focus.
apps.spoken: Sorting these papers is monotonous, so let's put on some music.
apps.writing: Use monotonous to show that sameness is the problem, not difficulty.

cloze.s: Sorting the same pile of envelopes for hours was ___, and Jo's mind began to wander.

cloze2.s: The speaker's ___ voice never rose or fell, and half the audience drifted off to sleep.

misuse.s: Her monotonous day was full of surprises, new faces, and changing plans.
misuse.why: Monotonous means always the same; surprises and changing plans are the opposite.

visual.alt: A sleepy face above a long, straight road.

words.frame: A monotonous task is one that ___.

words.def: A long speech by one person, with no one else speaking.
words.ex: In the play, the king delivered a monologue about his fear of losing the crown.
words.ex2: My uncle's monologue at dinner lasted so long that his soup went cold.
words.nonExample: A quick back-and-forth chat between two friends is not a monologue.

apps.academic: A monologue in a play lets the audience hear one character's private thoughts.
apps.spoken: Sorry, I was on a monologue; what do you think?
apps.writing: Use monologue for one speaker talking at length; use dialogue for two or more.

cloze.s: While the other actors stood silent, the hero spoke a ___ that lasted five minutes.

cloze2.s: The teacher's ___ went on so long that no student had a chance to ask a question.

misuse.s: The two friends held a monologue, taking turns to answer each other's questions.
misuse.why: A monologue is one person speaking; two friends taking turns is a dialogue.

visual.alt: A theater mask beside a speaking face.

words.frame: A monologue is different from a dialogue because ___.

words.def: A very large number of people or things.
words.ex: A multitude of fans packed the stadium long before the gates opened.
words.ex2: The desert sky held a multitude of stars, far too many to count.
words.nonExample: Two people waiting at a bus stop are not a multitude.

apps.academic: A multitude of factors, not one cause, shaped the outcome.
apps.spoken: There was a multitude of people at the beach today.
apps.writing: Use a multitude of for a very large number; it is stronger than several.

cloze.s: A ___ of people lined the parade route, standing ten deep along the curb.

cloze2.s: The librarian faced a ___ of questions when the new database opened, far more than she could answer at once.

misuse.s: A single visitor showed up at the party, and the host said that one guest was a multitude.
misuse.why: A multitude is a very large number; one guest is not.

visual.alt: A crowd of people filling a stadium.

src.note: Taught as a whole word; the multi- part is visible but the ending is not taught as a separate part.

words.def: Having many sides, parts, or aspects.
words.ex: Climate change is a multifaceted problem involving energy, farming, cities, and weather.
words.ex2: She was a multifaceted artist who painted, wrote songs, and built furniture.
words.nonExample: A problem with exactly one simple cause is not multifaceted.

segs.m: one flat side of a gem, or one side of an issue

apps.academic: Historians describe causes of war as multifaceted: politics, money, and fear all matter.
apps.spoken: It's a multifaceted question, so I can't answer in one sentence.
apps.writing: Use multifaceted to signal that you will discuss more than one side of a topic.

cloze.s: Poverty is a ___ problem; housing, jobs, health, and schools all play a part.

cloze2.s: The ___ writer composed poems, directed plays, and taught science to children.

misuse.s: It was a multifaceted problem with only one simple cause that anyone could name.
misuse.why: Multifaceted means having many sides; one simple cause is the opposite.

visual.alt: A cut gem next to a puzzle piece.

passage.title: Two Towns, One River
paras: Everyone in the towns of Ridgeway and Pine Hollow agreed on one fact: the Little Fork River was drying up. The trouble began when Ridgeway's mayor announced a unilateral plan to build a dam without asking Pine Hollow, which sat downstream. Within a week, a multitude of angry residents had gathered on the bridge between the towns, holding signs and shouting questions.

A calmer approach came from the state capital. Two lawmakers, one from each major party, formed a bipartisan committee and invited both mayors to bilateral talks in the old grange hall. Ana Ortiz, a seventh grader who had written about the river for her school paper, was allowed to sit in the back and take notes.

The first morning was monotonous. An engineer delivered a forty-minute monologue about water levels, and the only sounds besides his voice were scratching pencils. Ana nearly fell asleep until he mentioned that the Valley Water Company, which held a monopoly on the pipes in both towns, was losing a third of its water to leaks.

That detail changed the discussion. The problem was multifaceted: leaking pipes, a dry climate, thirsty farms, and prices set by a company with no competitor all played a part. Ana thought of her favorite author, a Pine Hollow writer whose fantasy trilogy about a river spirit had taught her that a stream belongs to many people at once.

By Friday the committee proposed repairing the pipes first and delaying the dam. When the clerk called the roll, every mayor and council member said yes, and the vote was unanimous. Ana closed her notebook and wrote one last line: agreement is slower than a unilateral decision, but it lasts longer.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the phrase “unilateral plan” most nearly means a plan made by
choices: both towns together
the state government
one side acting alone
a group of engineers
qs.why: The mayor announced the dam without asking Pine Hollow, so only one side decided.

qs.q: Why does the narrator call the first morning of talks monotonous?
choices: Everyone argued loudly about the dam.
The lawmakers refused to attend.
A long speech with little change filled the room, broken only by scratching pencils.
The talks took place outdoors in bad weather.
qs.why: Monotonous means dull because it stays the same, and the forty-minute speech and quiet pencils give that picture.

qs.q: Which detail changed the direction of the discussion?
choices: The crowd gathered on the bridge.
The company that held a monopoly on the pipes was losing a third of its water to leaks.
Ana's notes about the school paper.
The clerk calling the roll on Friday.
qs.why: The text says that detail changed the discussion, and it led the committee toward repairing pipes.

qs.q: Why does the committee propose repairing the pipes before building the dam?
choices: The dam would cost less than repairs.
Pine Hollow had asked for the dam first.
The engineer said dams never work.
Fixing the leaks might save water without a dam.
qs.why: Because so much water was leaking, repairing pipes might solve part of the shortage more cheaply and without harming the downstream town.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Rivers always dry up in the summer.
Seventh graders should run town meetings.
Water companies should be shut down.
Working together on a many-sided problem can lead to a lasting agreement.
qs.why: The talks move from a unilateral plan to bilateral talks and a unanimous vote, and Ana's last line says agreement lasts longer.

write.prompt: Imagine two groups in your school disagree about a rule. Describe how a bilateral conversation could help, and use at least three words from this unit.
write.frame: If one group decided alone, ___. Instead, a bilateral talk could ___, and the result might be ___.

study.task: Choose three words from the unit that start with different prefixes. For each, split off the prefix, say what number it names, and test whether that number matches the meaning. Mark one word where the parts help only a little and explain why.

multitude : crowd

given: They told one story about a lost island.
Readers waited years for the last one.
combine.model: Readers waited years for the last book of the author's trilogy, a connected story about a lost island.

discuss: Is a unilateral decision ever the right choice? Use unilateral and bilateral.
Why might a bipartisan solution last longer than one made by a single party?
Which unit word could you use to describe a play, a problem, and a crowd? Explain your choice.
produce.explain: Explain the difference between a monologue and a dialogue. Use both words and give one example from a book, show, or class discussion.

argue.prompt: Claim: One company should never hold a monopoly on an essential service such as water or electricity. Take a side and support it with two reasons that use words from this unit.
argue.frame: I believe that a monopoly on ___ is ___ because ___. Customers without a choice may ___.

constructed.prompt: Two schools need to decide how to share a gym. Describe one unilateral way and one bilateral way to decide, then say what a unanimous result would look like. Use all three words.
look: shows that unilateral means one side alone and bilateral means two sides together
constructed.model: A unilateral way would be for one school to post a schedule without asking. A bilateral way would be for both schools to meet and agree on days. A unanimous result would mean that every person in both groups voted yes.

constructed.prompt: Describe a class, a speech, or a story that was monotonous and then explain how a multifaceted version would be different. Use monotonous and multifaceted.
look: gives a concrete detail of sameness
explains variety or many sides in the better version
constructed.model: The science lecture was monotonous because the teacher read the same kind of slide in the same flat voice. A multifaceted lesson would mix demonstrations, group questions, and stories so that students see the topic from several sides.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words built on the number prefixes uni-/mono-, bi-, tri-, and multi-. They split each word, name the number, and test the result against the real meaning, then read a narrative about two towns and a river that uses all ten words.

notes.va.unanimous.adj: Model uni- plus anim plus -ous as 'of one mind', then check it against the definition. Contrast with majority and overwhelming. A common error is calling a large majority unanimous.
notes.va.unilateral.adj: The visible base lateral means side. Draw two stick figures and an arrow from only one. Ask who was left out and whether the decision was still legal or fair; those are different questions.
notes.va.bilateral.adj: Pair with unilateral on a two-column chart. Introduce multilateral as the next step on the ladder. In anatomy bilateral also means both sides of the body; mention it only if students raise it.
notes.va.bipartisan.adj: Bipartisan is used for two major political parties in the United States. Distinguish from partisan (strongly loyal to one party). Keep the discussion on structure, not on any current politics.
notes.va.trilogy.n: Check the parts tri- plus -logy, but note that -logy here means a set of works rather than the study of something. Students may think any three-book series is a trilogy even when it grew to four.
notes.va.monopoly.n: Distinguish the economic term from the board game. The word poly in monopoly comes from a Greek word about selling and is not the prefix poly- meaning many; teach the word part honestly. Ask what customers lose without competition.
notes.va.monotonous.adj: Build from mono- plus tone plus -ous: one tone, no change. Have a student read a sentence in a flat voice, then with variety, to hear the difference.
notes.va.monologue.n: Contrast with dialogue. Students often think monologue is just a long speech by anyone; stress that no one else is speaking. Connect to plays and to a speaker's private thoughts.
notes.va.multitude.n: Treat multitude as a whole word: multi- is visible but the ending is not taught as a part. Have students replace a multitude of with many and decide what is lost.
notes.va.multifaceted.adj: Show a cut gem to explain facet, then connect to a problem with many sides. The figurative step from gem to idea is worth saying out loud. Avoid using it as a simple synonym for good.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: “Bilateral. I see bi-, which means two, and lateral, which means side. So two sides. The sentence says two countries signed it, so two sides fits. Unilateral has uni- for one: one side alone, like the mayor deciding about the dam without asking the town downstream.”
discuss: Which prefix in the unit was easiest to use, and which word broke the pattern the most?
How does the number of voices in a decision change whether people accept it?
misconceptions: Mono- always means bad or boring.
Bi- always means exactly two years or weeks, as in a recurring event.
A trilogy is any long story.
extend: Add words with the same prefixes from other classes (monorail, triathlon, multimedia) and sort them by how closely the parts predict the meaning.
Write a one-page scene in which a unilateral decision is replaced by a bilateral agreement, using at least four unit words.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Link back to research words: ask students to cite and compile a list of number-prefix words from their texts, and to judge whether each source is reputable. Revisit unilateral, bilateral, and unanimous two days later in a short sort, again at one week, and use the ced/cess unit later in the year to compare how a root behaves across prefixes.

wida.oral: Partner A reads a clue such as 'one speaker talking for a long time' without naming the word. Partner B names the unit word and points to the prefix that helped.
